name: Voice transformation software
lead: Voice transformation software changes the pitch or timbre of a speaker's voice, in real time or in post-processing. Wikipedia describes voice changers as hardware or software that alters pitch or timbre or adds distortion, with software versions now very common and using many algorithms.[1] The sources reviewed contain no community discussion of its use for appearance or content creation.
Pitch alteration is described as key to changing a male voice to female or the reverse, and voice cloning software can mimic a specific person from recordings.[1]

paras: Early voice changers were electronic devices, often used on phones for disguise.[1] Pitch correction was rare until 1997, when Antares introduced Auto-Tune, developed by Andy Hildebrand using autocorrelation methods from seismic mapping. Hardware units later allowed live use.[2] Earlier, engineers had used the Eventide Harmonizer in the late 1970s.[2]
Documented uses include anonymity in documentaries and fictional depictions in media.[1] Extreme pitch-correction settings produced a robotic effect popularised by a 1998 song.[2]

card.summary: Software that shifts voice pitch or timbre, used for disguise, effects and content; no appearance-related evidence reviewed.
card.note: Effects apply only to the processed audio, not the user's actual voice.

quick.overview:
Voice transformation tools alter the pitch and tone of recorded or live speech.

Sources reviewed describe general uses like anonymity and music production.
quick.mechanism: Algorithms change the amplitude, pitch and tone of the audio signal, and cloning tools model a particular person's voice.
quick.risks: Voice cloning is associated in reference sources with social engineering concerns.
